questions.q: The Task API supports CRUD. Which routes are those?
questions.explain: CRUD is the four basic things you do with records. The API maps them to POST /tasks, GET /tasks and GET /tasks/:id, PATCH /tasks/:id and DELETE /tasks/:id.
options: Create, read, update and delete: POST, GET, PATCH and DELETE on tasks
Compose, route, use and deploy
Only GET /tasks and GET /health
Connect, request, upload and download

questions.q: What is a middleware in this lesson?
questions.explain: Middleware is how work that applies to every request (logging, headers, auth) is written once. next() runs the rest of the chain.
options: A function (ctx, next) that can act before and after the rest of the chain, or stop it by not calling next
A server that sits between the client and your API
A package you must install to handle requests
A route handler that only answers GET requests

questions.q: Why does the logger go first in the middleware list?
questions.explain: Middleware runs in the order you list it. A logger placed after the auth check would never see the rejected requests, which are often the ones you want to see.
options: So it sees every request, including those that a later middleware such as requireApiKey rejects
Because compose only allows one middleware before the handler
So that it runs after the response has been sent
The order does not matter; middleware all run at the same time

questions.q: Why should routes throw errors and let one middleware turn them into responses?
questions.explain: If each route writes its own error responses, one of 50 routes will eventually send a stack trace or a file path to the client. One error handler means one place to get it right.
options: With many routes, one will get its error answer wrong; one place keeps every answer consistent and stops leaks in 500 responses
Because res.end cannot be called inside a route
Because throwing is faster than returning
So the server restarts after every error

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only an HttpError, thrown on purpose with a message written for the client, is shown as it is. Anything else is a bug or an outage: the client gets a plain 500 and the details go to the server log.

questions.q: A database call fails with connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.7:5432 (db password rejected). What should the client see?
questions.explain: That message contains an internal address and a hint about a password. Log the details where you can read them; tell the client only that something went wrong.
options: A 500 with {"error":"Internal Server Error"}; the full message goes to the server log
A 500 with the full error message, so the client can report it
A 500 with the stack trace, so developers can debug faster
A 200 with an empty list, so the client does not notice

questions.q: Why does loadConfig(env) take the environment as a parameter instead of reading process.env itself?
questions.explain: A function that receives its inputs is easy to test. server.js is the only file that touches process.env and the port.
options: So a test can pass a plain object, while server.js passes process.env
Because process.env cannot be read inside a module
So the API key is copied into the code
Because process.env is only available in the browser

questions.q: Why does loadConfig push each problem into a list and throw once at the end?
questions.explain: Throwing at the first problem makes you restart, fix, restart, fix. Collecting them gives you the whole list in one go.
options: So you see every problem at once, instead of fixing one per restart
Because throw can only be used once per file
So the server can start even when some settings are wrong
So the problems are saved to .env

questions.q: What does the Task API do when TASKS_API_KEY is missing?
questions.explain: A server without its secret is not safe to run, so it stops at once with a clear message. A key is never written into the code, and never printed in a log.
options: It prints the configuration problem and refuses to start (process.exit(1))
It starts with a default key written in the code
It starts with no key, so every route is public
It generates a new key and prints it in the log

questions.q: How does the lesson give the server its API key on your computer?
questions.explain: The key is made with crypto.randomBytes(32), kept in .env, and kept out of Git. Secrets never go into code or into files you commit.
options: A random key in a .env file, loaded with --env-file-if-exists=.env, and .env listed in .gitignore
A key written into src/config.js and committed
A key typed into package.json under "scripts"
The key "secret", which is fine for development

questions.q: The lesson says you will later replace store.js with a database "and nothing else will need to change". What makes that possible?
questions.explain: The Map is private (#tasks). As long as a new store offers the same methods, the routes do not care where the tasks live.
options: The rest of the app only calls the store's methods (list, get, create, …), never the Map inside it
Databases and Map objects are the same thing
The store is written in a database language
The app reads tasks.json directly as well

questions.q: Why does requireApiKey use timingSafeEqual instead of given === apiKey?
questions.explain: A normal comparison answers a tiny bit faster when the first characters are wrong. timingSafeEqual always takes the same time, so there is nothing to measure.
options: === stops at the first different character, so an attacker can measure response times and discover the key one character at a time
=== cannot compare strings longer than 32 characters
timingSafeEqual also checks that the key has not expired
=== is case-insensitive, so "ABC" would equal "abc"

questions.q: timingSafeEqual needs two inputs of the same length. What does this print?
questions.explain: Inputs of different lengths make timingSafeEqual throw. Hashing both sides first gives two 32-byte values, which can always be compared, and also hides how long the real key is.

questions.q: This copies how requireApiKey reads the header. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only a header that starts exactly with "Bearer " gives a key; slice(7) removes those 7 characters. Anything else, including a missing header, gives an empty string, which never matches the real key.

questions.q: requireApiKey(apiKey, ["/health"]) skips the key check for /health. Which mistake would be a security problem?
questions.explain: Forgetting a public path only makes one route stricter. Adding a path by mistake opens it to everyone. Keep the public list as short as possible.
options: Adding "/tasks" to the public list by accident, which exposes every task without a key
Leaving "/health" out of the list, so the health check needs the key
Putting the middleware after securityHeaders
Sending WWW-Authenticate: Bearer with the 401

questions.q: When is one shared API key not enough?
questions.explain: A shared key says "this caller is one of ours", not who they are. An API used by many people needs real user accounts, passwords and permissions.
options: When many people use the API: each needs their own account and permissions, so they can only do what they are allowed
When the API is called by your own programs only
When the key is longer than 32 characters
When the server runs on port 3000

questions.q: What do the headers X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Cache-Control: no-store tell a browser?
questions.explain: These are cheap safety headers. nosniff stops the browser treating data as a different type (such as a script), and no-store keeps private data out of caches.
options: Don't guess the content type of the response, and don't keep a cached copy of the task data
Encrypt the response, and delete it after reading
Only accept JSON requests, and block other origins
Retry the request if it fails, and store the result on disk

questions.q: Why does PATCH /tasks/:id refuse any field except title and done?
questions.explain: Accept only the fields you expect. Copying whatever arrives lets a client change things it must not touch, such as ids or owners.
options: If the store copied every field, a client could send {"id": 1} and overwrite another task's id
Because JSON bodies may only have two fields
To make the request body smaller than the limit
Because Object.assign only works with two fields

questions.q: In the Task API, parseId throws notFound (404) for /tasks/abc, not 400. Why is that reasonable?
questions.explain: /tasks/abc names a task that cannot exist, so 404 describes it well. The important part is that the text is checked before it is used.
options: No task can ever have the id abc, so "not found" is a true answer about that URL
Because 400 is only for server errors
Because the router cannot throw 400
Because abc might become a valid id later

questions.q: What are SIGINT and SIGTERM?
questions.explain: Signals are messages the operating system sends a process. The server listens for both and shuts down gracefully.
options: Signals from the operating system: Ctrl + C sends SIGINT, and Docker or a host sends SIGTERM to stop your app
Two kinds of HTTP request
Error codes, like ENOENT
Events that createServer emits for every request

questions.q: What does a graceful shutdown do?
questions.explain: server.close stops new connections and calls its function when the last one ends. Nobody gets cut off halfway through a request.
options: Stops accepting new connections, lets requests in progress finish, then exits
Exits at once, dropping every open request
Restarts the server with the same port
Sends a 500 to every client that is connected

questions.q: The shutdown code has setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10_000).unref(). What is it for?
questions.explain: Normally the program ends by itself once the last connection closes. If one never closes, the timer forces an exit. Without unref, the timer alone would keep the program running for 10 seconds.
options: A safety net: if a request hangs, give up after 10 seconds; unref stops the timer from keeping the program alive on its own
It restarts the server every 10 seconds
It makes every request wait 10 seconds before being answered
It deletes the API key after 10 seconds

questions.q: At 20,000 lines, createApp({ store, apiKey, logger }) has grown to 30 arguments: a database pool, a mailer, a cache, a payment client… Which pain point is this?
questions.explain: Creating and passing dependencies by hand grows with every service you add. Dependency injection, which ZudoJS provides, is the standard answer.
options: Wiring dependencies: who creates what, in which order, and how to swap a real one for a fake in a test
Routing by hand
Validation
No types

questions.q: Why does hand-written validation, like checkTitle and the PATCH allow-list, become a problem in a big API?
questions.explain: None of the checks is hard, but there are many, and consistency matters. That is why frameworks offer schema validation.
options: It must be written again for every field of every resource, each developer does it slightly differently, and one forgotten check is a bug or a security hole
Validation is only needed in small APIs
JavaScript cannot validate more than a few fields per request
Validation makes every request take more than one second

questions.q: Finish compose(middlewares, handler). It returns a function run(ctx). Each middleware is called as middleware(ctx, next), where next() runs the next middleware, and after the last one, handler(ctx).
questions.explain: Keep an index. If it has reached the end of the list, call the handler; otherwise call the middleware at that index with a next that runs the chain from index + 1.

questions.q: Finish the middleware onlyAdmins. When ctx.user is missing, set ctx.status = 401 and stop the chain. When the user's role is not "admin", set ctx.status = 403 and stop. Otherwise, call next.
questions.explain: No user means "who are you?" (401); a known user without the right role means "not allowed" (403). Returning without calling next stops the chain, so the handler never runs.

questions.q: Finish toResponse(error). For an HttpError, return { status: error.status, body: { error: error.message } }. For any other error, push its message into serverLog and return status 500 with the body { error: "Internal Server Error" }.
questions.explain: Use instanceof HttpError to tell errors you threw on purpose from bugs and outages. Only the log gets the real message with the file path; the client gets a plain 500.

questions.explain: Push each problem into an array and throw once at the end, so all of them are reported together. Use exactly these two messages. Note that the message names the key but never prints its value.

questions.q: Finish pickChanges(body) for PATCH. Throw unknown field "x" (with the real name) for any key other than title and done. done, if present, must be a boolean (else throw done must be true or false). title, if present, is trimmed. Return an object with only the fields that were sent.
questions.explain: Check every key against the allow-list first, then copy only the known fields, checking their types. Never copy the whole body into a stored record.

questions.q: Finish readLimit(query). Read limit from the query string with URLSearchParams; the default is 20. It must be 1 to 3 digits and from 1 to 100; otherwise return the text "400".
questions.explain: A missing value is null, so ?? "20" gives the default. Check the text with a pattern, then the range. The maximum stops one request from asking for everything.

questions.explain: Return an async (ctx, next) => { … } function. Count the total before await next(), and the failures after it, because only then is the status known.
